territorial_scope.description: Federal statute reaching employers engaged in commerce or an industry or activity affecting commerce.

evidence.quote: engaged in commerce or an industry or activity affecting commerce

summary.short: Bill barring employers from retaliating against covered employees and independent contractors who report AI security vulnerabilities or AI violations to regulators, law enforcement, Congress or supervisors. Enforced by Labor Department complaint or district court action, with reinstatement, double back pay and damages.
summary.long: The bill would prohibit any employer engaged in commerce from discharging, demoting, suspending, threatening, blacklisting, harassing or otherwise discriminating against a covered individual (employees, former employees, independent contractors and former independent contractors) because of protected disclosures about an AI security vulnerability or AI violation. Protected disclosures include information given to the appropriate regulatory official or the Attorney General, a regulatory or law enforcement agency, any Member of Congress or congressional committee, or a supervisor, and assistance in related investigations or proceedings. AI security vulnerability means a security failure that could allow emerging AI technology to be acquired by theft or other means. AI violation covers violations of federal law relating to AI and failures to respond to a substantial and specific danger to public safety, health or national security. A covered individual may file a complaint with the Secretary of Labor under the procedures of 49 U.S.C. 42121(b), or, if no final decision issues within 180 days, sue in federal district court with a jury trial, subject to limitation periods of 6 years, 3 years from knowledge of the facts, and an outer limit of 10 years. Prevailing individuals may receive reinstatement, two times back pay with interest, compensatory damages including litigation costs and attorneys' fees, and other remedies. These rights may not be waived or altered by contract, including mandatory arbitration. The text states no effective date and no civil penalty amounts.

thresholds.note: No numeric cutoff in the bill changes scope, eligibility, exemption, obligation tier, prohibition, benefit tier, penalty tier or price tier. The 180-day wait (Sec. 3(b)(1)(B)) and the 6-year, 3-year and 10-year limitation periods (Sec. 3(b)(2)(B)(ii)) are procedural time limits, not thresholds. The 2 times back pay remedy (Sec. 3(b)(3)(B)) is relief, not a cutoff. The employer definition has no numeric size test.
